outputs.L1:
The mountain sheep are sweeter,  
But the valley sheep are fatter;  
We therefore deemed it meeter  
To carry off the latter.

We made an expedition;  
We met a host, and quelled it;  
We forced a strong position,  
And killed the men who held it.

On Dyfed’s richest valley,  
Where herds of kine were browsing,  
We made a mighty sally,  
To furnish our carousing.

Fierce warriors rushed to meet us;  
We met them, and o’erthrew them;  
They struggled hard to beat us,  
But we conquered them, and slew them.

As we drove our prize at leisure,  
The king marched forth to catch us;  
His rage surpassed all measure,  
But his people could not match us.

He fled to his hall-pillars;  
And, ere our force we led off,  
Some sacked his house and cellars,  
While others cut his head off.

There, in bewildering strife,  
We spilt blood enough to swim in;  
We orphaned many children,  
And widowed many women.

The eagles and the ravens  
We glutted with our foemen:  
The heroes and the cravens,  
The spearmen and the bowmen.

We brought away from battle—  
And much their land bemoaned them—  
Two thousand head of cattle,  
And the head of him who owned them:

Ednyfed, King of Dyfed,  
His head was borne before us;  
His wine and beasts supplied our feasts,  
And his overthrow, our chorus.
outputs.L2:
The sheep that graze on the mountains may taste better,  
yet those in the valleys carry more flesh;  
so we judged it wiser  
to seize the valley flocks instead.

We set out on a raid,  
encountered an army, and crushed it.  
We stormed a fortified place  
and killed the men defending it.

In Dyfed’s most fertile valley,  
where cattle herds were feeding,  
we launched a great attack  
to stock our revels with provisions.

Brave fighters charged against us;  
we faced them and threw them down.  
They fought fiercely to defeat us,  
but we mastered them and killed them.

While we leisurely drove away our captured livestock,  
the king came out with his forces to stop us.  
His fury was beyond restraint,  
but his people were no match for ours.

He retreated to the pillars of his hall;  
and before our army withdrew,  
some of our men plundered his house and wine cellars,  
while others cut off his head.

In that chaotic struggle,  
we shed blood enough to swim through.  
We left many children without fathers  
and many women without husbands.

We fed eagles and ravens  
with the bodies of our enemies:  
the brave and the cowardly alike,  
the spearmen and the archers.

From the fight we carried away—  
to the deep grief of that land—  
two thousand cattle,  
along with the head of their owner:

Ednyfed, ruler of Dyfed.  
His head was carried before us;  
his wine and livestock filled our banquets,  
and his defeat became the song we sang.
outputs.L3:
The raiders chose the wealth of the valleys over the harsher rewards of the mountains. Rather than pursuing the sweeter mountain sheep, they set their sights on the fatter sheep of the fertile lowlands, where Dyfed’s prosperity was concentrated.

They launched an expedition into Dyfed and met armed resistance along the way. The defenders tried to stop them, but the raiders overcame them and seized a strong position from which they could press their attack. From there, they descended upon Dyfed’s rich valley, killing many warriors and driving off cattle to supply their feast.

When the king of Dyfed attempted to halt the raid, his forces were defeated. The raiders plundered his household, broke his power, and finally beheaded him. His death became the grim climax of the expedition, a sign of the raiders’ triumph and of Dyfed’s humiliation.

The poem celebrates this violent raid without softening its consequences. It presents the slaughter of warriors, the grief of widows and orphans, the theft of livestock, and the king’s severed head as marks of victory. In doing so, it turns devastation into heroic praise, glorifying the raiders’ courage, ferocity, and success.
outputs.L4:
The poem tells the story of a brutal cattle raid carried out against Dyfed. The attackers descend upon the land with clear purpose, choosing the fattest sheep from the valley and taking livestock by force rather than by right. Their raid is not merely an act of theft, but a military assault: they come armed, prepared to overpower anyone who stands in their way, and they use violence to seize what they want.

As the attack unfolds, the invaders plunder the king’s hall and crush all resistance. The wealth and security of Dyfed are stripped away, and the raid becomes a symbol of total devastation. The cattle, sheep, and treasures taken from the land represent not only material loss, but also the humiliation of a defeated kingdom. Those who attempt to defend the hall and its ruler are overcome, showing the destructive power of organized warfare.

The raiders return in triumph, driving two thousand cattle before them and carrying the severed head of King Ednyfed as a trophy of victory. Their celebration emphasizes the scale of their conquest, but it also reveals the poem’s darker meaning. Beneath the boasting and heroic language lies a stark image of war’s cruelty: a ravaged land, a fallen king, stolen wealth, and lives violently ended. The poem therefore presents the raid as both a moment of martial success and a reminder of the terrible human cost of conflict.
outputs.L5:
**The, But, And**

The smallest words can sometimes carry the greatest weight. **The** points us toward something specific, giving shape and focus to an idea. It turns a simple object into something known: *the book, the road, the moment*.

**But** introduces contrast. It reminds us that life is rarely simple or one-sided. We may have plans, **but** unexpected changes appear. We may face challenges, **but** we can still move forward.

**And** connects. It brings thoughts, people, and possibilities together. It shows continuation and growth: hope **and** courage, effort **and** success, today **and** tomorrow.

Together, **the**, **but**, and **and** may seem like ordinary words, but they help build meaning. They guide our sentences, shape our stories, and connect the many parts of human experience.

We forced a strong position,

They struggled hard to beat us;  
But we conquered them, and slew them.

As we drove our prize at leisure,  
The king marched forth to catch us:  
His rage surpassed all measure,  
But his people could not match us.  
He fled to his hall-pillars;  
And, ere our force we led off,  
Some sacked his house and cellars,  
While others cut his head off.

We there, in strife bewildering,  
Spilt blood enough to swim in:  
We orphaned many children,  
And widowed many women.  
The eagles and the ravens  
We glutted with our foemen;  
The heroes and the cravens,  
The spearmen and the bowmen.

We brought away from battle,  
And much their land bemoaned them,  
Two thousand head of cattle,  
And the head of him who owned them:  
Ednyfed, king of Dyfed,  
His head was borne before us;  
His wine and beasts supplied our feasts,  
And his overthrow, our chorus.
